In the time before sound knew its own voice, there lived a lonely mountain spirit named Kira. She dwelt in the highest peaks where clouds gathered, and though she could see the world below—villages celebrating, children laughing, lovers whispering—she could hear nothing. Silence was her eternal companion.

The boy heard his own song return, changed somehow—sweeter, sadder, full of longing. He smiled, understanding he was not alone.

From that day forward, Kira learned to catch every sound that reached her peaks and send it back transformed. This is why mountains return our voices, and why echoes sound like both ourselves and something other—the grateful reply of a spirit who finally learned to speak through listening.

Where the first tear touched the ground, it did not disappear. Instead, it began to sing—a soft, bubbling melody that had never been heard before. The tear called out to its siblings, and soon more tears joined the song, flowing together across the barren rock.

This was how the First River was born.

The River sang as it carved its path through mountains and valleys, and wherever it flowed, life awakened. Trees stretched their roots to drink its waters. Flowers bloomed along its banks. Animals emerged from the shadows to listen to its eternal song.

But the River grew lonely, for it could only flow in one direction, never able to return to the places it had been. So Aeluna gave it a gift: every drop of water would one day rise as mist, return to the sky, and fall again as rain, allowing the River to sing its song eternally.

This is why rivers still sing today, and why the rain tastes faintly of tears and remembering.
